narrative.text: Front cover and title page of 'Monitoring and Evaluating Digital Health Interventions: A practical guide to conducting research and assessment', co-published with the Johns Hopkins University Global mHealth Initiative.

Copyright and publication page for 'Monitoring and evaluating digital health interventions: a practical guide to conducting research and assessment' (WHO, 2016, ISBN 978-92-4-151176-6), detailing CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO licensing terms, suggested citation, Cataloguing-in-Publication data, third-party material policies, general disclaimers, and design and photography credits.

Table of contents listing front matter (Acknowledgements, Acronyms and abbreviations, Preface, Executive summary, Introduction), Chapters 1 through 6 and their subsections (covering M&E overview, claims and frameworks, monitoring, evaluation, data quality assessment, and the mERA reporting checklist), and Annex I (Glossary).

Acknowledgements page crediting authors and contributors from the WHO Department of Reproductive Health and Research (RHR), Johns Hopkins University Global mHealth Initiative (JHU-GmI), Duke University, United Nations Foundation (UNF), African Centre for eHealth Excellence, implementing partner organizations, the Innovation Working Group (IWG) Catalytic mHealth Grant Mechanism, Green Ink, and Norad.
First page of the Acronyms and abbreviations list (ANC through KEMRI), defining clinical, economic evaluation, health information system, and organizational abbreviations used throughout the Guide.
Second page of the Acronyms and abbreviations list (M&E through WHO), defining monitoring and evaluation, digital health, maternal and child health, study reporting, and agency abbreviations.

Preface situating the Guide within five years of collaborative learning across 26 mHealth projects supported by WHO RHR, UNF, Norad, and JHU-GmI, and outlining its pragmatic focus on monitoring deployment fidelity and evaluating outputs, health outcomes, and cost-effectiveness.

Executive summary explaining how monitoring and evaluation (M&E) needs evolve across digital health intervention maturity stages—from technical functionality and feasibility to usability, effectiveness, attributable impact, and value for money—and outlining the Guide's progression from value claims and indicators to data quality assessment and reporting.

Introduction to the Guide and Figure 1 ('The Guide Roadmap: six steps for the M&E of digital health interventions'), summarizing the contents of Chapters 1 through 6 across maturity stages, claims and frameworks, technical and process monitoring, qualitative/quantitative/economic evaluation designs, data quality assessment, and the mERA checklist.

Continuation of the Introduction distinguishing implementation monitoring (fidelity, quality, and coverage) from programme evaluation (attributing outputs, outcomes, and economic value), identifying the intended audience of implementers, researchers, and policy-makers, and defining the key term 'Digital health'.
Section divider title page for Chapter 1: Overview of monitoring and evaluation.

Opening of Chapter 1 introducing the intervention maturity life-cycle schematic (Figure 1.1), which illustrates how concurrent monitoring activities (functionality, stability, quality, fidelity) and evaluation activities (usability, feasibility, efficacy, effectiveness, implementation research, and economic/financial evaluation) evolve from prototype to national implementation.

Part 1a ('Defining goals for monitoring and evaluation'), defining process monitoring in digital health, explaining how inquiry graduates across the six stages of intervention maturity from device factors to user interaction and health system scale-up, and listing core monitoring questions on specifications, stability, consistency, site variation, and deployment benchmarks.

Box 1.1 mapping the six stages of the intervention maturity life-cycle (pre-prototype/prototype, pilot, demonstration, scale-up, and integration/sustainability) against monitoring goals, evaluation stages, user scale (10–100 to 100 000+), and measurement targets, followed by the definition of evaluation and the challenge of attributing extrinsic changes to the digital health intervention.

Continuation of Part 1a listing illustrative evaluation questions for measuring attribution across usability, efficacy, effectiveness, and cost, explaining how monitoring and evaluation complement each other, and defining the key terms 'Benchmark', 'Evaluation', and 'Process monitoring'.

Concluding paragraph of Part 1a explaining how poor implementation and weak process monitoring can confound evaluation results—illustrated by unreceived SMS reminders due to connectivity issues being mistaken for intervention ineffectiveness.

Part 1b ('Developing an M&E plan for your digital health intervention'), presenting the seven-step M&E pathway (Figure 1.2), defining the key term 'Claim', and detailing Step 1 on classifying the stage of maturity and corresponding stage of evaluation.

Continuation of Step 1 on formulating appropriate claims (distinguishing optimization of a validated health intervention from novel digital health interventions, summarized in Box 1.2), followed by Step 2 ('Develop an underlying framework') and Step 3 ('Identify evidence needs and evaluation objectives' using SMART criteria).

Box 1.3 listing the six steps for defining SMART M&E objectives, and Table 1.1 ('Linking stages of maturity with evaluation methods and claims') mapping Early (pre-prototype, prototype, pilot), Mid (demonstration), and Advanced (scale-up, integrated and sustained programme) maturity stages to evaluation stages and technology, intervention, and health claims.

Steps 4, 5, and 6 of the M&E planning pathway: finalizing an appropriate study design, deciding between internal and external evaluators (illustrated in Figure 1.3 across inputs, processes, outputs, outcomes, and impact), and weighing prospective versus retrospective evaluation timing.

Continuation of Step 6 on quantifying time and financial, human, and physical resources (Box 1.4, noting the 10% budget benchmark), followed by Step 7 ('Develop an M&E implementation plan') detailing required components: activities and sub-activities, responsible persons, timelines, and budgets.

Table 1.2 providing an illustrative format for an M&E implementation plan (monitoring antenatal care coverage and pregnancy outcomes via SOP development and staff training), followed by the Chapter 1 reference list (citations 1–9).
Section divider title page for Chapter 2: Setting the stage for monitoring and evaluation.

Opening of Chapter 2 outlining the three core M&E questions (goal, process organization, and measurement) and introducing Part 2a ('Articulating claims'), which defines 'Claim' and 'Value proposition' and explains how value propositions communicate end-user benefits relative to a comparator.

Continuation of Part 2a explaining how a claims-based approach aligns M&E objectives with stakeholder expectations, streamlines measurement, and guides indicator selection, illustrated by Box 2.1 (comparing a claim, evaluation objective, hypothesis, and indicator for SMS measles vaccination reminders) and introducing the two pathways for digital health claims.

Figure 2.1 and accompanying guidance distinguishing Pathway 1 (evaluating the added benefit of a digital health system in optimizing delivery of an already validated health intervention, focusing on process and coverage outcomes) from Pathway 2 (evaluating whether a novel digital health intervention directly and independently improves health outcomes).

Section on linking digital health claims with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and universal health coverage (UHC), featuring Table 2.1 which maps UHC determinant layers (accountability, supply of commodities/human resources/facilities, demand/contact/continuous coverage, quality/effective coverage, and cost/financial coverage) to digital health strategies and illustrative claims.

Overview of the five steps in a claims-based approach (Figure 2.2) and detailed guidance on Step i ('Map stakeholders'), explaining how to identify and prioritize decision-makers, project staff, end-users, and scientific or scale-up partners.

Steps ii through v of the claims-based approach: clarifying stakeholder expectations (with sample stakeholder interview questions in Box 2.2), articulating specific and measurable top claims per stakeholder, measuring claims through M&E and process documentation, and updating claims to match observed evidence.

First part of Table 2.2 ('Illustrative categories of digital health stakeholders and claims'), mapping government entities (e.g. ministries of health), private sector organizations/mobile network operators, donors, technical agencies (e.g. WHO), beneficiaries/clients, and NGOs to their roles, relevant claim categories, and example claim statements.

Continuation of Table 2.2 covering the digital health community (including technical working groups) and the scientific community, detailing their roles as peers and future adopters along with relevant claim categories and illustrative claim statements.

Part 2b ('Developing an M&E framework'), introducing the role of frameworks in conceptualizing project goals, activities, and outcomes, and defining the key terms 'Conceptual framework', 'Results framework', 'Logical framework/logic model', 'Theory of change', 'Inputs', 'Processes', and 'Outputs'.

Guidance on constructing a conceptual framework (illustrated in Figure 2.4 connecting intervention X through intermediate factors A, B, and C to anticipated goal Z), definitions of 'Outcomes' and 'Impact', and a pointer to K4Health framework toolkits (Figure 2.3).

Table 2.3 comparing the description and purpose of conceptual frameworks, results frameworks, theories of change, and logical frameworks, followed by detailed guidance and the first three steps for building a results framework.

Steps 4–6 for creating a results framework and Box 2.3/Figure 2.5 describing the Mobile Technology for Community Health (MOTECH) initiative in Ghana (comprising the Mobile Midwife voice messaging service and the nurse-facing Client Data Application) and its five immediate results.

Figure 2.6 presenting the illustrative results framework for MOTECH in Ghana, linking the overall project goal ('Improve maternal and child health') to five immediate results (IR1–IR5), lower-level results (LLR2a–b, LLR4a–b), and specific quantitative indicators.

Detailed explanation of logical frameworks (logic models) in digital health M&E, defining and distinguishing technology, programmatic, and policy inputs; implementation and supervision processes; technological and service delivery outputs; health system, provider, and client outcomes; and medium- to long-term health and financial impacts.

Figure 2.7 presenting an illustrative logic model for the MomConnect maternal health SMS initiative in South Africa, mapping partnerships, health promotion messaging, facility/community, technology, and funding inputs and processes to outputs, outcomes, and mortality reduction impacts.

Box 2.4 and Figure 2.8 describing how South Africa's MomConnect initiative registers pregnant women via USSD at clinics to deliver stage-based maternal and infant health SMS messages, followed by an introduction to Theory of Change models and the six core questions required to test them.

Minimum required components of a Theory of Change (context, causal pathway of outcomes/preconditions, intervention sequence, assumptions, and diagram/narrative summary) and a Further Reading box citing foundational references on conceptual frameworks, results frameworks, and theories of change.

Part 2c ('Setting the stage: selecting indicators for digital health interventions'), defining the key terms 'Functionality', 'Indicator', 'Usability', and 'Users', introducing qualitative and quantitative indicators (recommending 10–15 per programmatic area), and presenting the Specific and Measurable components of the SMART criteria.

Continuation of Part 2c completing the SMART indicator criteria (Attainable, Relevant, Time-bound), explaining how indicator selection shifts along a 'barometer' (Figure 2.9) between process indicators (for interventions of known efficacy) and outcome indicators (where an evidence base is absent), and introducing the four-part indicator classification framework.

Figure 2.10 ('Categorization of digital health indicators') organizing indicators around four sequential questions—Does the technology work? How do people interact with the technology? How does the technology improve the process? How do improvements in service delivery affect health?—accompanied by Box 2.6 on the PRISM framework and an introduction to Functionality indicators.

Discussion of technical factors and qualitative software quality assessments (including ISO/IEC 25000:2014 SQuaRE criteria), alongside Table 2.4 listing sample functionality indicators across technical factors (connectivity, power, skilled local staff, maintenance, functionality) and organizational factors (staff training hours).

Discussion of organizational factors and primary/secondary data sources for functionality indicators, followed by the 'Usability – How do people interact with the technology?' section covering functional and service output indicators, behavioural factors, and core questions on user coverage, user response, and user adoption.

Table 2.5 listing sample usability indicators across user coverage, user response, and user adoption, followed by discussion of back-end digital data sources and user surveys, and Figure 2.11 illustrating the iterative spiral feedback loop between technology performance and user interaction.

Section on 'Process improvement – How does the technology improve service delivery?', introducing Figure 2.12 on addressing cost, efficiency, quality, and utilization constraints across health system, provider, and client levels, and defining client-level indicators.

Case study and monthly monitoring chart (Figure 2.13) for FHI 360's Mobile for Reproductive Health (m4RH) SMS programme in Kenya and Tanzania, followed by definitions of provider-level and health-system-level indicators (aligned with the six WHO health system building blocks) and client/system cost constraint considerations.

Tables 2.6 and 2.7 (beginning) of Chapter 2 Part 2c, listing client-level indicators across efficiency, quality, utilization, and costs (with explanatory footnotes on averted incidences, contact modes, adequacy definitions, and out-of-pocket cost savings) and provider-level efficiency and quality indicators for measuring how digital health technology improves the implementation process.

Continuation of Table 2.7 (provider-level utilization and cost indicators and footnotes) and Table 2.8 of Chapter 2 Part 2c, detailing health-system-level efficiency, quality, utilization, and cost indicators for assessing how digital health technology improves implementation processes across facilities and target populations.

Constraint and measurement considerations in Chapter 2 Part 2c for health-system-level cost savings (monetizing staff and client time gains and operational efficiencies) and for collecting and interpreting technical efficiency, quality of care (structure, process, and outcome dimensions), and service utilization/coverage indicators across client, provider, and health system levels.

Guidance on evaluating health outcomes (Question 4 of the M&E framework: 'How do improvements in service delivery affect health outcomes?'), explaining when evaluation can focus on process and early outcome indicators rather than established downstream health impacts, alongside a 'Further Reading' box of standardized RMNCAH indicator repositories (Every Woman Every Child, CORE Group, and DHS).

Continuation of the Chapter 2 Part 2c 'Further Reading' box listing standardized indicator repositories and guides for HIV programmes (UNAIDS, MEASURE DHS), malaria programmes (DHS Malaria Indicator Survey, President's Malaria Initiative), health service delivery and quality of care (WHO, MEASURE Evaluation SPA), and cross-cutting MEASURE Evaluation indicator summaries.

Chapter 2 References list (citations 1–17), covering value proposition and business model design resources (MaRS), CommCare, evaluation design and mHealth UHC frameworks (Habicht et al., Mehl & Labrique), stakeholder engagement methodologies (Bryson et al., Gable & Shireman), M&E frameworks and Theory of Change guides (UN Women, USAID, World Bank, DFID, MLE, WHO, K4Health, Earp & Ennett), and the MOTECH Ghana case study.

Conclusion of the Chapter 2 References list (citations 18–35), covering the GSMA mHealth impact model, South Africa's MomConnect, Malawi SC4CCM, ISO/IEC 25000 SQuaRE software quality standards, MEASURE Evaluation and PRISM/ePRISM frameworks, Boehm's spiral model, mHealth evidence and pilot studies (Labrique et al., FHI 360 m4RH, A.T. Kearney), WHO health system building blocks, technical efficiency (Palmer & Torgerson), and quality of care (Donabedian).
Title page for Chapter 3: 'Monitoring digital health interventions'.

Introduction to Chapter 3 on process monitoring of digital health interventions, featuring the 'How will this chapter help me?' overview box, Key Terms definitions ('Process monitoring', 'Monitoring burden', and 'Users'), and an overview of how the four monitoring components (functionality, stability, fidelity, and quality) evolve across intervention maturity stages.

Box 3.1 defining the four major components of digital health monitoring (Functionality, Stability, Fidelity, and Quality) with their guiding questions, Figure 3.1 illustrating concurrent monitoring and evaluation components across the intervention maturity life-cycle from prototype to national implementation, and the start of guidance on identifying target inputs by distinguishing primary and secondary users.

Continuation of Chapter 3 guidance on identifying target monitoring inputs versus outputs and outcomes, including Box 3.2 contrasting primary users (who enter data or use clinical algorithms) with secondary users (who receive SMS reminders or educational calls) and emphasizing the quality of technical, training, and behaviour change inputs.

Chapter 3, Part 3a ('Identifying stages of intervention maturity'), explaining how resource allocation and monitoring priorities shift from technical functionality and stability in early maturity stages to workforce standardization, fidelity, and quality in middle and late stages, illustrated by Figure 3.2 ('Relative monitoring burden by component across intervention maturity stages').

Chapter 3, Part 3b ('Tools for monitoring'), presenting Box 3.3 ('Raw materials checklist') and describing how human-centered design (HCD), software requirements specifications (SRS), use case narratives, and wireframes support system development and process monitoring.

Description of quality assurance (QA) test cases in Chapter 3 Part 3b and Figure 3.3 ('Illustrative examples of business process flows and SRS', adapted from PATH's Better Immunization Data Initiative), showing a patient immunization record query workflow and SRS requirement items (10.5–10.20) for evaluating and merging duplicate vaccination events.

Completion of Chapter 3 Part 3b covering back-end data structures and metadata (timestamps, GPS, non-events), codebooks (data dictionaries), indicators lists, and real-time data dashboards, illustrated by Figure 3.4 ('cStock's monitoring dashboard').

Introduction to Chapter 3, Part 3c ('Digital health process monitoring components') and Table 3.1 ('Summary of process monitoring components'), comparing Functionality, Stability, Fidelity, and Quality across monitoring timing, guiding questions, potential measures, technical/user/implementation categories, and monitoring burden by maturity stage.

Detailed guidance on monitoring Functionality in Chapter 3 Part 3c, covering what to monitor (skip patterns, validation checks, form schedules, UI, data exports, dashboards), how to monitor using QA test cases (illustrated in Table 3.2 with pass/fail scenarios for client registration and Polio-1 vaccination scheduling), who will monitor, and when to monitor.

Completion of the Functionality monitoring section in Chapter 3 Part 3c—explaining how to use pre- and post-launch testing findings to resolve bugs and document service disruptions for evaluation, and how functionality monitoring differs across maturity stages—accompanied by Figure 3.5 highlighting stages 2 and 3 (prototype/pilot and demonstration).

Detailed guidance on monitoring Stability in Chapter 3 Part 3c, covering what to monitor (server outages, SMS failure rates, application crashes, peak load responsiveness), how to monitor via server logs and automated alerts, who will monitor, when to monitor, how to use downtime findings, and how to automate stability monitoring across maturity stages.

Conclusion of Stability monitoring during scale-up and introduction to monitoring Fidelity in Chapter 3 Part 3c, dividing fidelity monitoring into three broad categories—(a) technical fidelity (uptime, SMS failure rates, form transmission, completion times), (b) external barriers (power banks, app updates, device loss/damage, data/SMS credits), and (c) user compliance.

Completion of the Fidelity monitoring section in Chapter 3 Part 3c, detailing user adherence indicators (form submission frequency, post-training app operation, clinical protocol compliance), automated server alerts and targeted retraining ('How to monitor'), supervisory and project manager roles ('Who will monitor'), continuous timing ('When to monitor'), corrective actions ('How to use monitoring findings'), and dashboard automation at scale ('How to monitor differently by maturity stage').

Start of the Quality monitoring section in Chapter 3 Part 3c, distinguishing (a) user capabilities (technical literacy, data entry accuracy, service consistency, timestamp/GPS regularities) and (b) intervention content quality (alignment with evidence-based guidelines and local context), and describing pre-launch trainee competency checklists and post-launch outlier tracking.

Completion of the Quality monitoring section in Chapter 3 Part 3c—covering formative testing of intervention messaging, who monitors user competency and content quality, when to monitor, using findings for real-time retraining and content refinement, and scaling quality monitoring across maturity stages—alongside Figure 3.6 ('Quality control checks on user ability to operate digital health system' from KEMRI's TextIT project).

Conclusion of maturity-stage considerations for Quality monitoring and start of an applied Chapter 3 case example of a pilot infant immunization SMS reminder and vaccinator registration system, illustrating (a) primary (health worker) versus secondary (family) user interactions, (b) maturity-stage priorities, and (c) pre-launch functionality QA test cases.

Conclusion of the Chapter 3 infant immunization SMS pilot example—illustrating pre-launch and ongoing stability monitoring for server downtime, SMS failure rates, and high-volume campaign loads—followed by the first part of the Chapter 3 References list (citations 1–6).

Continuation and conclusion of the Chapter 3 References list (citations 7–19 across pages 73–74), covering formative mHealth messaging (Maar et al.), K4Health glossary, user-centered design (McCurdie et al., IDEO), PATH logistics and BID Initiative requirements, IEEE SRS templates (Wiegers), usability.gov use cases and wireframing, PMNCH ICT workbook, JSI cStock, frontline worker mHealth adoption (Kaphle et al.), and SMS tone testing (Pollard et al.).
Title page for Chapter 4: 'Evaluating digital health interventions'.

Introduction to Chapter 4 on evaluating digital health interventions, including the 'How will this chapter help me?' overview box, the Key Term definition of 'Evaluation', and definitions of the five evaluation stages aligned with intervention maturity: Feasibility, Usability, Efficacy, Effectiveness, and Implementation research.

Chapter 4, Part 4a ('Key concepts for conducting digital health evaluations'), contrasting efficacy ('Can it work?' under ideal controlled conditions) with effectiveness ('Does it work?' in real-world settings across outputs, outcomes, and impact in Box 4.1) and defining implementation research and hybrid effectiveness–implementation approaches.

Box 4.2 outlining Curran et al.'s Type 1, Type 2, and Type 3 hybrid effectiveness–implementation trial designs, an introduction to formative versus summative evaluations, and a Key Terms glossary defining 'Implementation research', 'Formative evaluations', 'Summative evaluations', 'Experimental studies', 'Randomized controlled trial (RCT)', 'Observational studies', and 'Hierarchy of study designs'.

Overview of formative evaluations (needs assessments and process/implementation evaluations) and summative evaluations (outcome and impact evaluations), accompanied by Table 4.1 ('Formative versus summative evaluations') comparing objectives and illustrative questions across needs assessment, process evaluation, implementation evaluation, performance/outcome evaluation, impact evaluation, economic evaluation, secondary analysis, and meta-analysis.

Table 4.2 ('Types of study designs') in Chapter 4 Part 4a, comparing descriptions, advantages, and limitations across Analytic Experimental designs (individually and cluster randomized controlled trials, quasi-experimental studies), Analytic Observational designs (cohort, cross-sectional, case–control), and Descriptive designs (surveillance, cross-sectional surveys, ecological correlational studies, case reports, and case-series reports).

Discussion of descriptive and analytic study designs in Chapter 4 Part 4a, including Table 4.3 ('Qualitative research – study designs' covering case study, grounded theory, phenomenology, ethnography, and historical designs) and an explanation of experimental studies and randomized controlled trials (individual and cluster randomization).

Figure 4.1 ('Classes of descriptive and analytic study design', adapted from Brown & Lilford, 2006 and Grimes & Schulz, 2002), providing a taxonomy tree of descriptive studies (surveillance, ecological correlational, cross-sectional, case/case-series, and qualitative designs) and analytic studies (experimental RCTs and quasi-experimental designs, and observational cohort, cross-sectional, and case–control designs).

Table 4.4 ('Hierarchy of evidence by stage of evaluation'), ranking study designs by confidence in the strength of evidence (Excellent, Good, Fair, Poor) across Feasibility/Usability, Efficacy, Effectiveness, and Implementation Science stages, alongside Figure 4.2 illustrating a stepped-wedge study design across participant clusters and time periods.

Continuation of Chapter 4 Part 4a discussing complex RCT designs (stepped-wedge advantages, contamination risks, and analytical complexity), quasi-experimental designs, observational study types (cohort, case–control, cross-sectional), hierarchies of study designs, and the start of 'Linking inferences with study designs and methods'.

Guidance in Chapter 4 Part 4a on linking research questions and study designs to strength of inference, featuring Figure 4.3 ('Types of inference/study design': Descriptive, Exploratory, Analytic, Explanatory, and Predictive) and defining Habicht et al.'s three analytic inference levels: adequacy, plausibility, and probability.

Table 4.5 ('Linking inferences with study designs and methods', first part), mapping Descriptive, Exploratory, and Analytic (Adequacy, Plausibility, and Probability) inference types to their descriptions, research questions, limitations, study designs, and qualitative, quantitative, and mixed research methods.

Conclusion of Table 4.5 covering Explanatory and Predictive study inferences (descriptions, research questions, limitations, study designs, and quantitative/qualitative/mixed methods such as agent-based and econometric modelling, scenario-building, and Delphi techniques) and summary guidance on selecting analytic and explanatory inferences for digital health evaluations.

Introduction to Chapter 4, Part 4b ('Evaluation methods'), summarizing qualitative, quantitative, mixed-methods, and financial/economic evaluation approaches, with a 'Further Reading' box (WHO evaluation practice handbook and World Bank Impact evaluation in practice), a Key Terms box (FGDs, IDIs, structured observations, and participatory action research), and the start of the Qualitative methods section.

Continuation of Qualitative methods in Chapter 4 Part 4b, contrasting open-ended qualitative guides with closed-ended quantitative questionnaires and detailing structured observations—including vaccination clinic and CHW shadowing examples and step-by-step procedures before, during, and after observation.

Advantages and disadvantages of structured observations (including Box 4.3 comparing subjective versus objective note-taking at a vaccination clinic) and detailed guidance on conducting in-depth interviews (IDIs), covering use cases with policy experts and patients on sensitive topics, persona development, interview guides, audio recording, and field notes.

Strengths and limitations of IDIs, detailed guidance on conducting focus group discussions (FGDs)—including group composition, moderator and note-taker roles, and Box 4.4 ('Example FGD questions for community health workers using a digital health system')—and the start of sampling strategies for qualitative methods (purposive and snowball sampling).

Completion of qualitative research methods in Chapter 4 Part 4b—covering purposive and snowball sampling, transcription and field notes, CAQDAS tools (Atlas.ti, QSR-Nvivo, MAXQDA, HyperRESEARCH), and deductive versus inductive analysis—followed by the introduction to Quantitative methods and single-question Polls (via SMS, IVR, USSD, or web).

Conclusion of Polls and detailed guidance on Surveys in Chapter 4 Part 4b, listing the seven steps for planning and conducting a survey and presenting Table 4.6 ('Reasons for conducting surveys with community-based clients and health-care providers').

Survey administration modes, sample size considerations, and start of sampling for survey data collection in Chapter 4 Part 4b, featuring Box 4.5 ('Examples of digital data collection platforms that can be deployed on mobile devices': CommCare, Magpi, Medic Mobile, ONA, OpenDataKit, RapidPro, and TextIT) and Box 4.6 ('Factors influencing sample size').

Classification of probability sampling methods (simple random, systematic random, stratified random, cluster random, and multi-stage sampling) and non-probability sampling methods (convenience, purposive, and snowball sampling), overview of quantitative data analysis and statistical software (Excel, STATA, SAS, SPSS), and the first part of Table 4.7 comparing qualitative and quantitative approaches.

Conclusion of Table 4.7 ('A comparison of qualitative and quantitative approaches' across data types, analysis purposes, sample sizes, and sampling techniques) and detailed guidance on Mixed-methods approaches in Chapter 4 Part 4b, including digital health examples, triangulation advantages, design challenges, and Box 4.7 ('Checklist for the reporting of mixed-methods studies').
